interest: This document is of interest to economic and diplomatic historians of interwar Japan as it highlights two major facets of Japan's vital silk trade during the Great Depression. First, it notes the financial dependency of filatures on banking credit to purchase cocoons from agrarian producers, illustrating the tight nexus between rural distress and manufacturing finance. Second, it documents the market complications arising from the Japanese Government's interventionist disposal of surplus silk stocks to prominent American silk dealer Paolino Gerli, demonstrating the transnational repercussions of Japanese silk policy. Furthermore, it illustrates State Department recordkeeping practices where significant economic and commodity reports were cross-referenced to the general political affairs file (894.00).
overview: This file consists of a single Department of State 'List of Papers' docket sheet (Form DS-46) under subject classification 894.6225 (Silk Culture -- Japan). The sheet records two 1932 communications originating from Edwin L. Neville at the U.S. Embassy in Japan that were cross-referenced to broader political files (894.00/59 and 894.00 P.R./54). These entries summarize key economic conditions in the Japanese sericulture sector, notably the reliance of silk filatures on bank financing to purchase cocoons from farming communities, and the industry complications that followed the Japanese Government's bulk sale of raw silk stocks to American importer Paolino Gerli.

subfiles.summary: This document is a Department of State List of Papers (Form DS-46) indexing cross-referenced correspondence under class 894.6225 (Silk Culture -- Japan). The first entry indexes Telegram No. 107 of 1932 from Edwin L. Neville, noting that the Japanese silk industry is primarily agricultural and that reeling filatures rely on periodic bank credit to finance cocoon purchases from farmers (filed under 894.00/59). The second entry indexes Despatch No. 634 of June 1, 1932, from Neville concerning complications in the silk industry resulting from the Japanese Government's sale of silk to Paolino Gerli (filed under 894.00 P.R./54).
